teachings.quote: Just as a solid rock is not shaken by the storm, even so the wise are not affected by praise or blame.
teachings.reflection: Ground yourself before the day's weather arrives. Praise and blame are both just wind.
teachings.story:
The Dhammapada is a collection of verses attributed to the Buddha, preserved in the Pali Canon — and verse 81 is one of its plainest images. A mountain, the verse says, is not stirred by storms or by the wind's flattery; in the same way, a person grounded in understanding is not stirred by praise or blame.

The image works because it does not ask you to stop the weather. Storms of opinion — a reviewer's harsh line, a colleague's praise, a stranger's contempt — will keep coming. The practice is in what you are made of when they arrive. A rock doesn't resist the storm; it simply isn't the kind of thing a storm can move.

The commentary tradition adds that this equanimity is not indifference. The Buddha was famously warm and engaged. The stillness is at the center, not the surface: you can respond fully to what the day needs while refusing to hand your peace to whoever happens to be judging you this morning.
teachings.source: Dhammapada, verse 81 (Pali Canon); wording varies by translation

teachings.reflection: Expertise is useful until it becomes a lid. Make room for the thing you don't already know.
teachings.story:
A university professor came to the Zen master Nan-in to ask about Zen. Nan-in served tea. He poured the visitor's cup full — and then kept pouring. The professor watched the overflow until he could no longer restrain himself: 'It is overfull! No more will go in!'

'Like this cup,' Nan-in said, 'you are full of your own opinions and speculations. How can I show you Zen unless you first empty your cup?'

The story comes down through Paul Reps' classic collection '101 Zen Stories' (1939), and like most Zen lore it is a teaching tale rather than documented history. Its point survives the skepticism: a mind already full has no room for what is being offered. This is why the Zen tradition speaks of shoshin, beginner's mind — the open, slightly astonished attention of someone encountering something for the first time. It is the same stance a good scientist keeps toward data that disagrees with a favored model: not empty-headed, but empty-handed.
teachings.source: Zen lore, told of the master Nan-in; popularized by Paul Reps, 101 Zen Stories (1939)

teachings.quote: It's a poor thief who visits me tonight — I wish I could give him this beautiful moon.
teachings.reflection: Set down what was taken, what was lost, what was never yours. The best things cannot be stolen.
teachings.story:
Ryōkan (1758–1831) was a Japanese Zen hermit and poet who lived in a small hut on a mountain, owning almost nothing. One night a thief came and found there was almost nothing to take. Ryōkan returned, caught him in the act, and — the story goes — helped him carry out the few things worth taking, then sat outside in the moonlight, too warm now to sleep indoors.

'That poor fellow,' he wrote in a poem afterward. 'I wish I could have given him this beautiful moon.'

The anecdote is hagiography — polished by generations of admirers — but it points at something verifiable in Ryōkan's actual poems: a man who had genuinely little, and wanted less. The moon he could not give away is the standing image for everything that is already free. Tonight's losses — the argument you didn't win, the thing that slipped away — are the thief's bag. The moon is still there.
teachings.source: Told of the hermit-poet Ryōkan Taigu (1758–1831); Zen hagiography, reflected in his poems

teachings.quote: Nothing in the world is softer than water, yet nothing is better at overcoming the hard and strong.
teachings.reflection: Force is not the only form of power. Patience, position, and softness wear through stone.
teachings.story:
Chapter 78 of the Tao Te Ching observes a paradox: water, the softest thing in the world, defeats the hardest. Dripping water hollows stone; a flood moves boulders. Everyone knows this, Laozi says, yet no one applies it — we still believe strength means rigidity.

Alan Watts, who spent his last book on exactly this chapter, called the Tao 'the Watercourse Way': the course, the flow, the drift of nature. Water does not fight the rock; it finds the crack, the low place, the path of least resistance — and given ten thousand years, it owns the whole canyon. Watts loved to point out that the natural world doesn't 'push the river': the river pushes itself.

The practice is not passivity. It is refusing to spend yourself on head-on collisions when a softer angle accomplishes more. In an argument, in research, in a difficult season — be where the water is: patient, low, moving.
teachings.source: Laozi, Tao Te Ching, chapter 78; see Alan Watts, Tao: The Watercourse Way (1975)
teachings.videoLabel: Alan Watts reads Tao: The Watercourse Way

teachings.quote: Am I a man who dreamt of being a butterfly, or a butterfly dreaming I am a man?
teachings.reflection: Your view of the world is a view from somewhere. Hold it lightly.
teachings.story:
Zhuangzi, the wittiest philosopher of the Taoist tradition, ends a passage of his second chapter with a dream: he was a butterfly, fluttering happily, doing exactly as it wished — with no memory of being Zhuangzi. Then he woke, and there he was, solidly Zhuangzi. But, he writes, he could not tell: had he been Zhuangzi dreaming he was a butterfly, or was he now a butterfly dreaming he was Zhuangzi?

This is usually read as a puzzle about reality's uncertainty. It is better read as a joke about certainty. The whole chapter argues that every standpoint is partial — the 'this' and the 'that' depend on where you stand. The butterfly dream doesn't ask you to doubt the world; it asks you to notice how fluently you forget that your version of things is one version.

For a scientist this is almost professional hygiene: the map is not the territory, the model is not the phenomenon. Zhuangzi just says it with better wings.
teachings.source: Zhuangzi, chapter 2 (Qi Wu Lun), ~4th century BCE

teachings.quote: Before I studied Zen, mountains were mountains. While I studied Zen, mountains stopped being mountains. After enlightenment, mountains are mountains again.
teachings.reflection: Confusion is not failure — it is the middle of the road. What you knew simply, you will know simply again, but deeper.
teachings.story:
This famous saying is attributed to Qingyuan Weixin, a Tang-dynasty Ch'an master, and preserved in Dogen's records: thirty years before, mountains were mountains and waters were waters; then, studying Zen, mountains were no longer mountains; and finally, having attained rest, mountains are once again mountains.

The movement is the teaching. First, the naive view: things are just what they are, seen without depth. Then, analysis — this is where training, questioning, and doubt dissolve the obvious. The mountain is mostly empty space, a process, a name we pin on a process. Everything solid melts. Many people stop here and think the melting is the insight.

The third stage is the return: the mountain is again a mountain — but now you know what it cost to see it that way. It is the same trajectory as a scientific education: the world before physics, the world of formalism, and then the practiced eye that sees the moon and the inverse-square law in the same glance, without confusion.
teachings.source: Attributed to Qingyuan Weixin, Tang dynasty; recorded by Dogen

teachings.quote: Your duty is to be — and not to be this or that.
teachings.reflection: Beneath the roles and the CV, there is the one noticing them. Get acquainted.
teachings.story:
In 1896, a sixteen-year-old boy in South India, Venkataraman, was seized by a sudden fear of death. He lay down, froze his body, and reasoned: the body is dying, but something here is fully aware of the dying — that awareness cannot be what dies. The fear dissolved. He left home shortly after and spent the rest of his life near the holy mountain Arunachala, becoming known as Ramana Maharshi.

His instruction was almost aggressively simple. Whatever arises — thought, mood, sensation — turn and ask: to whom does this appear? The answer is always 'to me.' Then the real question: who is this 'I'? Don't answer it with words; trace the sense of 'I' back toward its source and rest there. He called it atma-vichara, self-inquiry, and insisted it needed no ritual, no posture, no belief.

The quote above is from his recorded talks: your duty is to be, not to be this or that. Not self-improvement — self-attention.
teachings.source: Ramana Maharshi, from his recorded talks (e.g., Be As You Are, ed. David Godman)
teachings.videoLabel: Rupert Spira on self-inquiry and 'Who am I?'

teachings.quote: Tat tvam asi — That thou art. You are that which you seek.
teachings.reflection: The distance between you and what matters most may be an assumption worth testing.
teachings.story:
In the Chandogya Upanishad, the young Shvetaketu returns from years of study full of book-knowledge, and his father Uddalaka quietly dismantles his pride with a series of analogies — sleep, thirst, hunger, honey gathered from many flowers, and the seed of the banyan tree. Each time he concludes with the same words: tat tvam asi, that thou art. You, at your root, are not different from the fundamental reality the texts point to.

The same Upanishad also tells the cautionary tale of Indra and Virochana, gods who went to study under Prajapati. Both first settled for the reflection in a mirror — the body — and went away satisfied. Only Indra came back, troubled, and kept asking until he was shown something subtler than any object.

The phrase became one of the mahavakyas — the 'great sayings' — of Advaita Vedanta, and a millennium of commentary has unpacked it. But Uddalaka's delivery to his son is the original setting: not a doctrine to believe, but a pointer offered with love, meant to be tested in one's own experience.
teachings.source: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8.7 (and 6.1–6.2 for the tale of Indra and Virochana)
teachings.videoLabel: Swami Sarvapriyananda on Tat Tvam Asi (Vedanta Society of New York)

teachings.quote: Wisdom tells me I am nothing. Love tells me I am everything. Between the two, my life flows.
teachings.reflection: You are smaller than your worries and larger than your ambitions. Rest in the space between.
teachings.story:
Nisargadatta Maharaj (1897–1981) ran a small beedi shop — hand-rolled cigarettes — in a crowded lane of Bombay, above which he kept a modest room where visitors from around the world would sit on the floor and ask questions. He had been a householder, a father, a shopkeeper; after his guru's single instruction — 'you are not what you take yourself to be; hold to the sense I am' — he practiced for a few years and reported that everything changed while nothing external did.

The quote is from 'I Am That,' the book of his recorded conversations. It condenses the whole non-dual teaching into a rhythm you can live by. As pure awareness, you are nothing — no object, no boundary, nothing that can be threatened. As the life in all beings, you are everything — no one is a stranger. The error, he kept saying, is stopping at either half. Wisdom alone is cold; love alone is blind. A human life is what happens in the flow between them.
teachings.source: Nisargadatta Maharaj, I Am That (recorded conversations, ed. Maurice Frydman)

teachings.quote: This being human is a guest house. Every morning a new arrival. Welcome and entertain them all.
teachings.reflection: Tonight's dark mood is a guest, not a resident. It was sent, it will leave, and it may pay its way.
teachings.story:
Jalaluddin Rumi (1207–1273) was a scholar in Konya until a wandering dervish, Shams of Tabriz, upended his life — a friendship so total that when Shams disappeared, Rumi's grief turned into forty thousand lines of poetry. He whirled as he recited; the Mevlevi 'whirling dervishes' descend from him.

'The Guest House' is from his Masnavi-era poems, best known in the West through Coleman Barks's free translations. Its image is patient psychology: every morning, something arrives — a joy, a depression, a meanness, 'some momentary awareness' — and knocks. The reflex is to bolt the door against the dark visitors. Rumi's counsel is the opposite: welcome them all, even 'a crowd of sorrows who violently sweep your house empty of its furniture.'

The line that redeems the whole poem: 'He may be clearing you out for some new delight.' The grief that empties you is sometimes making room. You rarely get to know which it is while it's happening — so, Rumi says, be grateful for whoever comes. Each has been sent as a guide from beyond.
teachings.source: Rumi, from his poems; translation by Coleman Barks, The Essential Rumi (1995)
teachings.videoLabel: Coleman Barks speaks The Guest House (from 1:10:31)

teachings.quote: I laughed when I heard that the fish in the water is thirsty.
teachings.reflection: Searching for what you are swimming in is the oldest comedy. Look at what's already present.
teachings.story:
Kabir (c. 1440–1518) was a weaver in Benares — a working craftsman who wrote razor-sharp couplets in the street language of the day, refusing both Hindu ritual and Muslim orthodoxy while honoring the reality behind them both. His line about the fish is a joke with a blade in it: a fish searching for water is absurd, and so is a person searching everywhere for what they are made of.

Rabindranath Tagore's 1915 translation, 'One Hundred Poems of Kabir,' carried this verse into English: 'I laughed when I heard that the fish in the water is thirsty. Ever hearing of water, it is dying of thirst.'

Kabir's target is not ordinary effort — he taught practice — but misdirected seeking: the pilgrimage to find elsewhere what is already functioning as your own awareness. The phrase 'ever hearing of water' is the sting. You have heard about peace, presence, God, the Self — heard, read, discussed. The fish's problem is not distance. It is recognition.
teachings.source: Kabir, tr. Rabindranath Tagore, One Hundred Poems of Kabir (1915)

teachings.quote: The moth that flies around the light knows something the moth on the wall will never know.
teachings.reflection: Understanding at a distance has a strict ceiling. Some things are known only by contact.
teachings.story:
In a tale Rumi tells in the Masnavi, a teacher moth addressed a gathering of moths about the nature of the flame. None had seen a flame, so he sent one to investigate. The moth circled the candle, reported back: 'It is bright.' — 'You have seen the light. But what about the heat? Go closer.' A second moth flew nearer, touched the flame's edge, and returned singed: 'It burns,' he said — but he had only brushed it. Finally a third moth flew straight in and did not return. The teacher said: he alone knows the flame. He made his report by becoming it.

The story is Sufi teaching lore about the difference between studying, approaching, and being consumed — the degrees of contact with what one loves most. It is not a recommendation for recklessness, but a diagnosis of distance: there are things — a craft, a love, a spiritual path, even a research problem — about which the observer's vocabulary simply runs out. If you want to know what the flame is, at some point you have to be the moth that doesn't come back.
teachings.source: Sufi teaching tale; told by Rumi in the Masnavi

teachings.quote: Nowhere can a man find a quieter or more untroubled retreat than in his own soul.
teachings.reflection: You don't need to go anywhere to step back. The retreat is portable; carry it into the evening.
teachings.story:
Marcus Aurelius was the most powerful man in the world, and he slept badly. The book we call 'Meditations' was never meant for publication: it is his private notebook, written in army camps on the Danube frontier between wars — a Roman emperor reminding himself, over and over, how to stay sane.

This passage, from Book 4, continues: retreat into yourself whenever you like; nowhere is quieter. And he adds a condition — renewal is only possible for a mind that is ordered, that keeps at hand 'the first principles' of what it is doing and why.

It is easy to romanticize a mountain cabin or a monastery. Marcus had none available. His retreat had to be interior, portable, openable in a tent between councils of war. The evening version is simple: instead of reaching for the phone, close the door of attention for five minutes and go to the one place noise cannot enter uninvited. He would insist on the 'uninvited' — the door has a latch, and you own it.

teachings.quote: Live the questions now. Perhaps you will then gradually, without noticing it, live along some distant day into the answer.
teachings.reflection: Not every problem yields to pressure tonight. Some resolve only by being lived.
teachings.story:
In 1903, a nineteen-year-old military cadet named Franz Xaver Kappus, unsure whether his poems were any good, mailed them — and his despair — to the poet Rainer Maria Rilke. Rilke wrote back: don't send your work out; ask yourself, in the quietest hour of your night, must I write? If the answer is yes, build your life around it. Their correspondence continued for years.

The most famous counsel came when Kappus pressed him about life's big unresolved questions. Do not now seek the answers, Rilke wrote, which cannot be given you because you would not be able to live them. 'Live the questions now.' The point is not anti-intellectualism — Rilke revered discipline and craft. It is about the ripening of certain answers: like fruit, they cannot be forced, only grown toward, and the growing is the living.

For anyone mid-way through a hard problem — a thesis, a career decision, a slow grief — the letter removes a weight: you are not late. You are in the question, and the question is doing quiet work.
teachings.source: Rainer Maria Rilke, Letters to a Young Poet, letter 4 (1903; tr. M.D. Herter Norton)

teachings.quote: Tell me, what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life?
teachings.reflection: The day is not a to-do list to survive. It is the actual substance of the one life.
teachings.story:
Mary Oliver spent decades walking the ponds and fields of Cape Cod, notebook in pocket, and described her work plainly: attention is the beginning of devotion. 'The Summer Day,' from House of Light (1990), tracks a grasshopper — 'the one who has flung herself out of the grass' — eating sugar from the poet's hand, washing her face, snapping her wings open and floating away. Only then comes the pivot: 'I don't know exactly what a prayer is. I do know how to pay attention, how to fall down into the grass... how to be idle and blessed.'

The famous last line is often quoted as inspiration-poster energy. In context it is more serious: after a poem that is entirely receiving — watching, kneeling, strolling — the question lands as an audit. What is all your doing for, if it does not include the capacity to notice a grasshopper?

Her practical mysticism needs no metaphysics: the world is astonishing to anyone who actually looks at it, and looking is a trainable skill. This morning counts as practice.
teachings.source: Mary Oliver, The Summer Day, in House of Light (1990)
teachings.videoLabel: Mary Oliver reads The Summer Day (Beacon Press)

teachings.quote: Waking up this morning, I smile. Twenty-four brand new hours are before me. I vow to live fully in each moment.
teachings.reflection: You have already arrived. The next twenty-four hours are the destination.
teachings.story:
Thich Nhat Hanh — Vietnamese Zen master, poet, peace activist exiled from his homeland for opposing the war — rebuilt a practice tradition around gathas: short verses recited with the breath to anchor awareness in ordinary acts. The waking gatha, recited before the first foot touches the floor, is the one above. His community, Plum Village, uses verses like it all day: 'Breathing in, I calm my body. Breathing out, I smile.'

His core phrase was 'I have arrived, I am home' — the insight that the habit of running toward a future moment of completion is the exhaustion itself. The point is not to stop planning; it is to stop believing that life happens at the end of the planning. 'We have spent so much of our time running and looking for something,' he taught. 'We may miss our appointment with life.'

The morning smile is not mandated cheerfulness; it is a physical cue — soften the face, and the mind follows. Twenty-four brand-new hours. That is the raw material of the entire day, and it is already here.
teachings.source: Thich Nhat Hanh, Plum Village gatha practice (e.g., Present Moment, Wonderful Moment)
teachings.videoLabel: Plum Village guided meditation: I Have Arrived, I Am Home
